_comment: Drafted replies keyed by tweet id. Edit freely; the review page reads these as starting text and sends whatever is in the box.

replies.2092427029727916415: The 30 nanometre figure is the real headline, not the 95 percent. Worth pressing on "no new waste stream" though: adsorption concentrates PFAS rather than destroying it, so regenerating the powder should leave a concentrated eluate that still has to go somewhere.
replies.2092413047948386313: It is certified to NSF 42, 53 and 401, which genuinely beats most pitchers: 53 covers lead and PFAS, 401 covers microplastics. What it is not is 58, the reverse osmosis standard. Keeping the minerals is the same property that leaves fluoride and nitrate in.
replies.2092556408747425822: There is a specific reason to expect that association even at zero causal effect. Tumour vasculature is leaky and disorganised, so circulating particles accumulate there preferentially. Higher levels in cancerous tissue can be downstream of the tumour, not upstream.
replies.2092643242126852216: The trap is what people buy next. Ceramic nonstick is a sol gel coating that wears faster than PTFE, so it gets replaced more often, and PFAS free on the box refers only to the coating. Bare stainless or cast iron is the version with nothing to wear off.
replies.2092616379299951101: The direction of the effect is what makes this hard to summarise. Depending on ageing and surface chemistry, plastics can either shuttle cadmium toward roots or sequester it away from them. Does the review land on which dominates under field conditions?
replies.2092450662227591602: The polymer backbone is the easy part. What decides whether this is edible is the additives: plasticisers, antimony catalyst residue from PET, flame retardants. Those do not necessarily break down in the same step, and they are what would need clearing.
